# CipherStick

> CipherStick (repository name: Bails) installs Bitcoin Core on Tails, the
> amnesic Linux system whose applications connect through Tor (except Tails'
> Unsafe Browser, which CipherStick doesn't use). It runs from one
> USB stick on computers that can start Tails: 64-bit Intel or AMD PCs, not
> Apple-silicon Macs or ARM machines. Wallet backups use codex32
> (BIP-93) shares through the separately maintained python-codex32 app. A
> CryoStick is a second CipherStick meant to stay offline; it signs
> transactions by QR code. CipherStick is alpha software, and CryoStick is
> newer and still experimental.

## Facts

- Install: start Tails, connect to Tor, run
  `git clone https://github.com/benwestgate/bails&&bails/b`. You need one USB
  stick of 32 GB or more, about 1 hour, pen and paper. There is no
  vendor hardware and no account. The hour covers installation; Bitcoin
  Core's initial sync continues afterwards and can take hours to days
  (weeks on 4 GB RAM computers with slow USB sticks), see docs/FAQ.md.
- Bitcoin Core: the official release, downloaded over Tor. python-codex32
  needs Core 32, so until 32.0 is stable a fresh install uses the signed
  32.0rc2 release candidate. By default its
  SHA256SUMS must carry at least 3 good signatures from Guix builder keys
  chosen by the CipherStick maintainers. The optional "More Verification"
  step raises the required signature count by one per round. Keys already
  imported, including the maintainers', count toward it, so it does not
  guarantee a signature from a builder the user picked. Core runs as a full node, so the
  balance is checked locally and the wallet's addresses are never sent to a
  third-party server. Transactions it sends are broadcast to the Bitcoin
  network over Tor.
- Storage: Core, its data, the wallets, CipherStick itself and python-codex32
  live in Tails Persistent Storage (the Persistent Folder, GnuPG and Dotfiles
  features), which is LUKS-encrypted. Anything outside the enabled
  Persistent Storage features is erased at shutdown.
- Backups: codex32 splits the wallet seed into k-of-n shares written by hand
  on paper. Any k shares restore the wallet. Fewer than k reveal nothing about
  the secret itself, the addresses or the balance. Every share carries the
  same short identifier, which python-codex32 derives by default from the
  wallet's master fingerprint, so a found share can be matched to a wallet
  whose fingerprint is already known. Each share has a checksum that a
  person can verify by hand, and the Codex32 paper worksheets can recover
  the seed with no computer at all. The restored wallet is a standard
  single-key Bitcoin Core descriptor wallet, so it does not depend on
  CipherStick to spend.
- Offline signing (experimental; docs/DESIGN_SCOPE.md still lists offline
  signing as future work, and the receive-address check is unfinished, see
  issue #312): a CryoStick checks Tails' Offline Mode at every login and
  shuts down if networking is on. Bitcoin Core starts from a separate
  autostart, so it may briefly run before that check stops it. Core and
  codex32 are kept on it, so it does not need to go online before each use.
  Updating its software still needs a network connection.
  PSBTs cross between the sticks as one QR code each (python3-qr and
  zbarcam from Debian). There is no multi-part QR, so a PSBT with many
  inputs can be too large to cross; a one-input payment is about 500
  bytes. The signing wallet can be kept in RAM only by naming it `/tmp/...`.
  It adapts Bitcoin Core's doc/offline-signing-tutorial.md: PSBTs move by
  QR code instead of USB, the signer is a copy of a CipherStick, and the
  signing wallet is filled from codex32 shares.
- Code to review on top of Tails and Core: about 1,600 lines of bash in this
  repository, plus python-codex32.
- Cloning a CipherStick to a friend's USB stick is planned. The Clone menu
  item currently shows "Coming soon".

## Who it fits

- People who want a private, self-validating Bitcoin Core wallet without
  buying dedicated hardware or installing an operating system on a computer.
- Savers who want backups that are safe when one copy is found, and who are
  willing to test an experimental offline signer (CryoStick) meant to keep
  keys off networked devices. It detects networking and shuts down rather
  than preventing it, so it relies on the user keeping it offline.
- People who would rather rely on published, reviewable code than type a
  long manual procedure correctly every time they spend. This applies to the
  online CipherStick. With a CryoStick, each spend still means typing two
  short QR commands on each stick until issue #312 scripts them.

## Who it does not fit (yet)

- Daily spending from a phone, or Lightning.
- Multisig with independent signers, or an inheritance policy that a
  coordinator enforces. Neither is supported today; see docs/DESIGN_SCOPE.md.
- Anyone who wants a company to call for support.
